danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Fra fyrst Sjtjerbátovs hus blev fangerne ført lige ned ad Jomfru-Marken, til venstre for nonneklostret, hen til en køkkenhave, hvor en pæl var rejst. Bag pælen var en frisk grav gravet i jorden, og nær pælen og graven stod en stor menneskemængde i en halvkreds. Mængden bestod af nogle få russere og mange af Napoleons soldater, der ikke var på vagt — tyskere, italienere og franskmænd i forskellige uniformer. Til højre og venstre for pælen stod rækker af franske tropper i blå uniformer med røde epauletter, høje støvler og sjako'er.

Fangerne blev stillet op i en bestemt orden ifølge listen (Pierre var den sjette) og ført hen til pælen. Flere trommer begyndte pludselig at rulle på begge sider af dem, og ved den lyd følte Pierre, som om en del af hans sjæl var revet bort. Han mistede evnen til at tænke eller forstå. Han kunne kun høre og se. Og han havde kun ét ønske — at det forfærdelige, der skulle ske, skulle ske hurtigt. Pierre så sig om på sine medfanger og betragtede dem.

De to første var straffefanger med ragede hoveder. Den ene var høj og tynd, den anden mørk, lodden og senestærk med en flad næse. Den tredje var en husslave, omkring femogfyrre, med grånet hår og en buttet, velnæret krop. Den fjerde var en bonde, en meget smuk mand med et bredt, lysbrunt skæg og sorte øjne. Den femte var en fabriksarbejder, en mager, gulsotfarvet knægt på atten i en løs frakke.

Pierre hørte franskmændene rådslå, om de skulle skyde dem enkeltvis eller to ad gangen. »Parvis,« svarede den kommanderende officer med rolig stemme. Der kom uro i soldaternes rækker, og det var tydeligt, at de alle skyndte sig — ikke som mennesker, der skynder sig med at gøre noget, de forstår, men som folk, der haster med at afslutte en nødvendig men ubehagelig og ufattelig opgave.
En fransk embedsmand med skærf trådte hen til højre side af fangerækken og oplæste dommen på russisk og fransk.

Derpå nærmede to par franskmænd sig de dømte og greb på officerens kommando de to straffefanger, der stod først i rækken. Straffefangerne standsede, da de nåede pælen, og mens man hentede sække, så de sig sløvt omkring som et såret dyr, der ser den jæger, der nærmer sig. Den ene korsede sig uophørligt, den anden kradsede sig på ryggen og trak på munden i noget, der lignede et smil. Med hastige hænder bandt soldaterne for deres øjne, trak sækkene over hovederne og surrede dem til pælen.

Tolv skarpskytter med musketter trådte ud af rækkerne med faste, regelmæssige skridt og standsede otte skridt fra pælen. Pierre vendte sig bort for ikke at se, hvad der ville ske. Pludselig hørtes en knaldende, rullende lyd, der forekom ham højere end det voldsomste tordenvejr, og han så sig om. Der var lidt røg, og franskmændene foretog sig noget ved graven med blege ansigter og skælvende hænder. To fanger mere blev ført frem. På samme måde og med lignende blikke så disse to forgæves på tilskuerne med kun en stum bøn om beskyttelse i øjnene, tydeligvis ude af stand til at forstå eller tro, hvad der skulle ske med dem. De kunne ikke tro det, fordi de alene vidste, hvad deres liv betød for dem, og derfor hverken forstod eller troede, at det kunne tages fra dem.

Igen ønskede Pierre ikke at se og vendte sig atter bort; men igen slog en forfærdelig eksplosionslyd hans ører, og i samme øjeblik så han røg, blod og de blege, skræmte ansigter hos de franskmænd, der atter foretog sig noget ved pælen med skælvende hænder, der hindrede hinanden. Pierre trak vejret tungt og så sig om med et spørgende blik. Det samme spørgsmål stod i alle de blikke, der mødte hans.

I ansigterne på alle russerne og på de franske soldater og officerer uden undtagelse læste han den samme forfærdelse, rædsel og indre konflikt, som var i hans eget hjerte. »Men hvem gør dog dette? De lider alle ligesom jeg. Hvem er det så? Hvem?« lyste det et øjeblik igennem hans sind.

»Skarpskytter fra 86. regiment, fremad!« råbte nogen. Den femte fange, ham ved siden af Pierre, blev ført bort — alene. Pierre forstod ikke, at han var reddet, at han og resten kun var bragt herhen for at overvære henrettelsen. Med stadig voksende rædsel og ingen følelse af glæde eller lettelse stirrede han på det, der foregik. Den femte mand var fabriksknægten i den løse frakke. I det øjeblik de lagde hånd på ham, sprang han forskrækket til side og klamrede sig til Pierre. (Pierre gyste og rev sig løs.) Knægten var ude af stand til at gå. De slæbte ham afsted, mens de holdt ham under armene, og han skreg. Da de nåede pælen, blev han stille, som om han pludselig forstod noget. Hvad enten han forstod, at det var nytteløst at skrige, eller troede det utænkeligt, at mennesker skulle dræbe ham, indtog han sin plads ved pælen og ventede på at få bind for øjnene som de andre, og som et såret dyr så han sig omkring med glimtende øjne.

Pierre var ikke længere i stand til at vende sig bort og lukke øjnene. Hans nysgerrighed og ophidselse nåede, ligesom hele mængdens, det højeste punkt ved dette femte mord. Ligesom de andre syntes denne femte mand rolig; han trak sin løse frakke tættere om sig og gned den ene bare fod mod den anden.

Da man begyndte at binde for hans øjne, rettede han selv på knuden, der trykkede bag på hovedet; og da de lænede ham op mod den blodstænkede pæl, lænede han sig tilbage og rettede sig, da han var utilpas i den stilling, justerede sine fødder og lænede sig atter tilbage mere bekvemt. Pierre tog ikke øjnene fra ham og gik ikke glip af hans mindste bevægelse.

Sandsynligvis blev der givet en kommando, og den blev fulgt af otte musketsalver; men hvor meget Pierre end anstrengte sig, kunne han bagefter ikke erindre at have hørt den mindste lyd af skuddene. Han så kun, hvordan arbejderen pludselig sank ned i rebene, der holdt ham, hvordan blodet viste sig to steder, hvordan rebene slappedes under den hængende krops vægt, og hvordan arbejderen satte sig ned med hovedet hængende unaturligt og det ene ben bøjet under sig. Pierre løb hen til pælen. Ingen standsede ham. Blege, skræmte mennesker foretog sig noget omkring arbejderen. Underlæben på en gammel franskmand med tykt overskæg skælvede, mens han løsnede rebene. Kroppen sank sammen. Soldaterne slæbte den klodset fra pælen og begyndte at skubbe den ned i graven.
De vidste alle tydeligt og sikkert, at de var forbrydere, der måtte skjule sporene af deres skyld så hurtigt som muligt.

Pierre kiggede ned i graven og så, at fabriksknægten lå med knæene tæt op mod hovedet og den ene skulder højere end den anden. Den skulder hævede og sænkede sig rytmisk og krampagtigt, men allerede blev der kastet jord på hele kroppen. En af soldaterne, der åbenbart led, råbte barsk og vredt ad Pierre om at gå tilbage. Men Pierre forstod ham ikke og blev stående ved pælen, og ingen jog ham bort.

Da graven var fyldt, blev der givet en kommando. Pierre blev ført tilbage til sin plads, og tropperne på begge sider af pælen gjorde halv-omkring og marcherede forbi den med afmålte skridt. De fireogtyve skarpskytter med afladte musketter, der stod i midten af cirklen, løb tilbage til deres pladser, efterhånden som kompagnierne passerede.

Pierre stirrede nu med sløve øjne på disse skarpskytter, der parvis løb ud af cirklen. Alle undtagen én sluttede sig til deres kompagnier. Denne ene, en ung soldat med dødbleg ansigt, sin sjako skudt bagud og sin musket hvilende på jorden, stod stadig ved graven på det sted, hvorfra han havde fyret. Han svajede som en fuld mand og tog nogle skridt frem og tilbage for at undgå at falde. En gammel underofficer løb ud af rækkerne, greb ham om albuen og trak ham hen til hans kompagni. Mængden af russere og franskmænd begyndte at spredes. De gik alle tavst bort med sænkede hoveder.
»Det lærer dem at sætte ild på,« sagde en af franskmændene.

Pierre så sig om mod den talende og så, at det var en soldat, der forsøgte at finde en form for lettelse efter det, der var gjort, men ikke var i stand til det. Uden at fuldføre, hvad han havde begyndt at sige, gjorde han en opgivende bevægelse med armen og gik sin vej.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: They led the prisoners straight from Prince Shcherbatov's house down the Virgin's Field, past the left side of the nunnery, to a kitchen garden where a post had been set up. Behind the post a fresh pit had been dug. A large crowd stood around both in a semicircle. It was made up of a few Russians and a great many of Napoleon's off-duty soldiers — Germans, Italians and Frenchmen in all sorts of uniforms. On either side of the post stood lines of French troops in blue uniforms with red epaulets, high boots and shakos.

They arranged the prisoners in the order of the list (Pierre was sixth) and marched them to the post. Drums suddenly started beating on both sides, and at the sound Pierre felt as if a piece of his soul had been ripped away. He could no longer think or understand. He could only hear and see, and he had a single wish: that the terrible thing that had to happen would happen quickly. He looked around at the other prisoners and studied them.

The first two were convicts with shaven heads. One was tall and thin. The other was dark, shaggy and wiry, with a flat nose. The third was a house serf of about forty-five, with graying hair and a plump, well-fed body. The fourth was a peasant, a strikingly handsome man with a broad light-brown beard and black eyes. The fifth was a factory hand, a thin, sallow boy of eighteen in a loose coat.

Pierre heard the French discussing whether to shoot the prisoners one at a time or two at a time. "Two at a time," the officer in command answered calmly. The soldiers' ranks stirred, and it was plain that they were all in a hurry — not the way people hurry to do something they understand, but the way they hurry to get through a task that is necessary, unpleasant and beyond their comprehension.
A French official in a sash came up on the right of the line of prisoners and read out the sentence in Russian and in French.

Then two pairs of Frenchmen went up to the condemned men and, on the officer's order, took the first two convicts in the line. When they reached the post the convicts stopped. While the sacks were being brought, they stared around blankly, like a wounded animal watching a hunter come closer. One kept crossing himself. The other scratched his back and made a movement of the lips like a smile. The soldiers blindfolded them with quick hands, pulling the sacks down over their heads, and tied them to the post.

Twelve sharpshooters with muskets stepped out of the ranks with a firm, even tread and halted eight paces from the post. Pierre turned away so as not to see what was about to happen. Suddenly there was a crackling, rolling roar that seemed to him louder than the most terrible thunder, and he looked around. There was some smoke, and the Frenchmen, pale and with trembling hands, were busy near the pit. Two more prisoners were brought forward. These two looked around vainly at the onlookers in the same way, with the same look, silently begging for protection. They plainly could not understand or believe what was going to happen to them. They could not believe it because they alone knew what their lives meant to them, and so they neither understood nor believed that anyone could take them away.

Again Pierre did not want to look and turned away. But again the sound of a terrible explosion hit his ears, and in the same instant he saw smoke, blood and the pale, frightened faces of the Frenchmen, who were again busy at the post, their trembling hands getting in one another's way. Breathing hard, Pierre looked around as if to ask what it all meant. The same question showed in every look that met his.

On the faces of all the Russians and all the French soldiers and officers, without exception, he read the same dismay, horror and inner conflict that filled his own heart. "But who is really doing this? They are suffering just as I am. Who is it then? Who?" flashed through his mind for an instant.

"Sharpshooters of the 86th, forward!" someone shouted. The fifth prisoner, the one next to Pierre, was led away — alone. Pierre did not understand that he was saved, that he and the others had been brought there only to watch the execution. With growing horror, and with no sense of joy or relief, he stared at what was happening. The fifth man was the factory boy in the loose coat. The moment they laid hands on him, he jumped aside in terror and clutched at Pierre. (Pierre shuddered and shook himself free.) The boy could not walk. They dragged him along, holding him up under the arms, and he screamed. When they got him to the post he fell quiet, as if he had suddenly understood something. Perhaps he understood that screaming was useless, or perhaps he found it unbelievable that men would really kill him. Either way, he took his place at the post and waited to be blindfolded like the others, and like a wounded animal he looked around him with glittering eyes.

Pierre could no longer turn away or close his eyes. His curiosity and agitation, like those of the whole crowd, reached their peak at this fifth killing. Like the others, this fifth man seemed calm. He wrapped his loose cloak tighter and rubbed one bare foot against the other.

When they began to blindfold him, he adjusted the knot himself, because it hurt the back of his head. Then they propped him against the bloodstained post, and he leaned back. Finding that uncomfortable, he straightened up, set his feet properly and leaned back again, more comfortably. Pierre never took his eyes off him and missed none of his slightest movements.

Someone probably gave a command, and eight muskets went off after it. But try as he might, Pierre could never afterward remember hearing the slightest sound of the shots. He only saw the workman suddenly sag against the cords that held him, blood appear in two places, the ropes go slack under the weight of the hanging body, and the workman sink down with his head hanging unnaturally and one leg bent under him. Pierre ran up to the post. No one stopped him. Pale, frightened men were busy around the workman. The lower jaw of an old Frenchman with a thick mustache trembled as he untied the ropes. The body collapsed. The soldiers dragged it clumsily away from the post and began pushing it into the pit.
All of them clearly and certainly knew that they were criminals who had to hide the traces of their crime as quickly as possible.

Pierre looked into the pit and saw the factory boy lying with his knees drawn up to his head and one shoulder higher than the other. That shoulder rose and fell in a steady, convulsive rhythm, but spadefuls of earth were already being thrown over the whole body. One of the soldiers, obviously in distress, shouted at Pierre in a harsh, angry voice to go back. But Pierre did not understand him and stayed near the post, and no one drove him away.

When the pit had been filled in, a command was given. Pierre was taken back to his place, and the lines of troops on both sides of the post made a half turn and marched past it at a measured pace. The twenty-four sharpshooters, their muskets discharged, were standing in the center of the circle. As the companies passed, they ran back to their places.

Pierre watched with dazed eyes as these sharpshooters ran out of the circle in pairs. All but one rejoined their companies. This one, a young soldier with a deathly pale face, his shako pushed back and his musket resting on the ground, still stood by the pit where he had fired. He swayed like a drunk, stepping forward and back to keep from falling. An old noncommissioned officer ran out of the ranks, took him by the elbow and dragged him to his company. The crowd of Russians and Frenchmen began to break up. They all went away silently, with their heads bowed.
"That'll teach them to start fires," one of the Frenchmen said.

Pierre looked round at the speaker and saw a soldier who was trying to find some relief after what had been done and could not manage it. He did not finish what he had begun to say. He made a hopeless gesture with his arm and walked away.
